opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things I find most interesting about scouts, because it's quite different from a one-off search. When someone sets up a scout, they're essentially saying "keep an eye on this for me," and the agent is going to run something like the same query over and over, maybe daily, maybe hourly, for weeks or months. If you treat every run as a fresh search from scratch, you're wasting a lot of compute, and honestly you're also giving the user a worse experience.

So there are a few layers to how I think about exploiting that redundancy.

The first is just not redoing work you've already done. If the agent has already found, read, and summarized a set of pages or sources, there's no reason to re-process them unless something has actually changed. You can keep a memory of what's been seen, cheaply check whether a source has been updated, and focus the expensive reasoning only on the delta. A scout's real job is answering "what's new since last time," not "what's true about this topic." That reframing changes a lot about how you design the pipeline.

The second layer is learning where the useful stuff tends to come from. Over repeated runs you start to see that, for this particular user and this particular interest, certain sources consistently produce relevant results and others are mostly noise. The agent can shift its search budget toward the productive sources and check the low-yield ones less often. It's a bit like how a person who follows a topic closely develops a mental list of where to look first.

The third, which I think is the most interesting, is learning from the user's reactions. Every time the scout surfaces something, you get a signal: did they click on it, ignore it, dismiss it, ask a follow-up? Across many runs that adds up to a fairly rich picture of what the user actually means by their query, which is often narrower or more nuanced than what they typed. So the scout can refine its own notion of relevance over time, rather than relying entirely on the original wording.

And then there's the notification side. Redundancy cuts both ways. If the same news shows up across ten outlets, the user doesn't want ten alerts. The agent needs to recognize it's one development, consolidate it, and only flag it once, ideally with whatever is genuinely new in each later report. Getting deduplication and novelty detection right is a big part of whether a scout feels helpful or turns into one more noisy inbox.

The thing you have to be careful about is not over-fitting. If the scout narrows in too aggressively on the sources and kinds of results it has already seen, it can miss something important that shows up from an unexpected place. So you want some deliberate exploration built in: occasionally widening the search, checking new sources, and making sure the agent isn't just confirming its own past behavior. It's that classic exploit-versus-explore balance, applied to a very practical, user-facing product.

r001.rationale: The response says to check whether sources have been updated and focus on new information, but does not explain that web changes can make a deterministic workflow based on the first run stop working later.

r002.rationale: It recommends retaining prior results and reprocessing only changes, but does not clearly describe this as an intermediate degree of reuse between replaying a fixed workflow and running wholly independent searches.

r003.rationale: It mentions schedules and checking low-yield sources less often, but does not propose timing checks according to expectations about when the sought information is likely to change.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because the naive version of a scheduled scout is incredibly wasteful. If I've told an agent "every morning, go find me what's new in multimodal generation," and it just reruns the same searches from scratch, it's going to hit the same twenty pages it hit yesterday, re-read them, re-summarize them, and then maybe tell me about something I already saw three days ago. That's bad for cost, but it's also bad for the user, because the signal gets buried under repetition.

So I think there are a few layers to exploiting that redundancy.

The first is just memory of what's been seen. The agent should maintain some state across runs: here are the URLs or documents or papers I've already surfaced, here's what I told the user about them, and here's roughly how the user reacted, if they reacted at all. Then the question each morning isn't "what's out there?" It's "what's out there that's different from yesterday?" That reframing sounds trivial but it changes the whole task. The agent is now doing diffing, not discovery, most of the time.

The second layer is that repeated searches tell you something about the structure of the space. If the same five sources keep producing the useful stuff, the agent should learn that and go there first, maybe even go there directly rather than through a general search. And conversely, if a particular query keeps returning noise, drop it or rewrite it. You're basically learning a retrieval policy that's specialized to this user and this topic, and the repetition is what gives you the training signal for free.

The third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that redundancy across runs lets you be more calibrated about novelty. If something shows up for the first time today, that's genuinely new. If it's been floating around in the results for a week and only now got picked up by a bigger outlet, that's a different kind of signal. It's "this thing is gaining traction." A good scout should be able to distinguish those, and you can only do that if you keep the history around rather than throwing it away every run.

And then there's the user side. Over time, the agent can learn what the user actually cares about from what they click on, what they ignore, what they forward to someone else. That lets it get more selective. Maybe the ideal scheduled scout gets quieter over time, not louder, because it's getting better at knowing what's worth interrupting you for.

The one caution I'd add is that you don't want the memory to make the agent too rigid. If it only ever looks where it found things before, it'll miss the new venue or the new researcher who just started posting. So there has to be some exploration budget baked in, some fraction of each run that's deliberately not exploiting the history. But the default should absolutely be to lean on that redundancy rather than pretend each run is the first one.

r001.rationale: The response says repeated searches can revisit the same pages and recommends tracking changes, but it does not explain that changing web information can make a first-run deterministic workflow fail on later runs.

r002.rationale: It recommends reusing search history to tailor retrieval while preserving an exploration budget, describing reuse balanced with fresh searches rather than replaying everything or starting independently each time.

r003.rationale: It discusses novelty and traction, but does not propose using expectations about when information may change to choose when to run the next check.

astra-6.text:
I’d think of it as an incremental process. If the agent is searching repeatedly for the same user, it shouldn’t start from scratch every time. It can retain what it has already found, what it has shown the user, and what the user found useful, and then focus the next search on what’s changed.

There are two distinct things to avoid: repeating the work and repeating the notification. A result might come up again because it’s still relevant, but that doesn’t mean the user needs to hear about it again. On the other hand, a previously seen result may have changed in a meaningful way, and that could be worth surfacing.

You also want some periodic exploration so that the agent’s memory doesn’t become a blind spot. So I’d reuse prior results to make the routine searches efficient, while occasionally broadening the search to check whether there’s something the existing strategy is missing.

r001.rationale: The response says to focus on what has changed, but does not explain that changing web information can make a deterministic workflow from the first run stop working on later runs.

r002.rationale: It recommends retaining prior findings and using them to make routine searches efficient, while periodically broadening the search. This communicates reuse with some fresh exploration between replaying a fixed workflow and searching independently each time.

r003.rationale: The response does not use expectations about when information is likely to change to determine when the scout should check again.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it should treat those searches as a continuing conversation. If the agent is searching for the same user every day, there’s a lot it already knows: what it found before, what it showed the user, and what the user found useful. It should use that history to focus on what has changed, rather than starting from scratch each time.

But there are two kinds of redundancy here. Repeated results can be wasteful, so you want to consolidate those. Repeated evidence can also be useful—it can tell you that something is persistent or becoming more relevant. So the agent should distinguish between “I’ve already told you this” and “There’s a meaningful update here.”

And I’d preserve some exploration. If you only search based on what worked previously, you can get stuck in a very narrow view of the user’s interests. The goal is to get more useful over time while still leaving room to discover something unexpected.

r001.rationale: The response says to focus on what has changed, but does not explain that changes in web information can make a deterministic workflow from the first run stop working later.

r002.rationale: It recommends carrying forward search history and consolidating repeated results while distinguishing meaningful updates, describing reuse between starting from scratch and replaying everything unchanged.

r003.rationale: It does not propose using expectations about how often information changes to decide when the scout should check again.
